items.body: Every jumbled pile of person has a thinking part that wondersWhat the part that isn’t thinking isn’t thinking ofShould you worry when the skull head is in front of you?Or is it worse because it’s always waiting where your eyes don’t go? They Might Be Giants came home to Brooklyn Steel on Saturday, May 30, closing out a three-night residency in the neighborhood where the Johns once lived cheap, wrote weird, and turned absurdity into a municipal service. The Bigger Show tour, true to its name, brought no opening act, no filler, no warm-up comedian in a cardigan (sorry, ghost of Shecky Greene): just an eight-piece contraption with Brooklyn’s Ambassadors of Love: John Flansburgh, John Linnell, Danny Weinkauf, Dan Miller, Marty Beller…and a three-man horn section: Dan Levine, Stan Harrison, and Mark Pender, ready to inflate every miniature TMBG universe until it could be seen from space. John Flansburgh. Photo: Alice Teeple John Linnell and “Main Squeeze.” Photo: Alice Teeple Across much of their discography, the gloom and mordant philosophy in They Might Be Giants’ lyrics can rival The Cure, Nick Cave, and The Smiths, though their existential unease usually arrives disguised in bright, buoyant arrangements that pull from klezmer, free jazz, polka, musique concrète, the madcap noodlings of Raymond Scott, and, apparently, the nonstop caffeine-current of Sparks. They have long been darlings of well-meaning misfits: people with overactive brains, social anxiety, and a bone-deep sense of isolation, all finding refuge in feeling understood, for once. The first set was devoted to 1988’s masterpiece Lincoln, the band’s second album and still one of the great documents of American brain-pop gone beautifully berserk. The second half cracked open the cabinet and let the creatures crawl out: deep cuts, fan favourites, later-period live detonations, bits of Mink Car, the big sing-along monsters, the jokes that somehow got sharper with age, and the songs that have spent decades proving that cleverness can survive contact with an actual stage, a bar line, and several thousand people who know the words. Beginning with Santa’s Beard, the band tore straight into Lincoln with the confidence of people who know the record by muscle memory but still enjoy finding loose wires in the walls. Stand on Your Own Head bounced in with a ridiculous little grin. Piece of Dirt kept its strange miniature cruelty intact. Where Your Eyes Don’t Go carried that old TMBG chill. Pencil Rain and Cowtown landed with manic precision. Then came The Stick. For the uninitiated, The Stick is Flansburgh’s long-serving stage prop, a piece of sacred tree solemnly – if sporadically – employed as percussion during Lie Still, Little Bottle since the late Eighties. They Might Be Giants have had plenty of oddball visual business over the years: giant heads of newsman William Allen White, a long-retired confetti cannon, puppets big enough to terrify children and drunk college kids alike – but The Stick has earned its own strange little kingdom, complete with audience chant. There it was again at Brooklyn Steel, made divine by repetition, timing, and Flansburgh’s deadpan commitment to behaving as though he had brought Excalibur itself. John Flansburgh with The Stick. Photo: Alice Teeple The best TMBG shows always remind you that the band’s comedy was never sprinkled over the songs after the real work was done. It is structural. Their timing is musical, their music spans pathos and comedy, and their jokes usually contain a trap door and a footnote. During the between-song patter, Flansburgh and Linnell talked about living in Williamsburg in the 1980s, right around the corner from what is now Brooklyn Steel, back when paying $100 in rent was both a blessing and a curse. Another bit found Linnell talking about having strained his throat from a spirited scream chorus, telling Flansburgh he now sounded like Brian Keith from Family Affair, then realizing in real time that only a narrow slice of the room had any clue what he meant. (Don’t worry, at least one did.) A woman near the front held up a sign that read PLAY BOAT OF CAR, asking for the beloved track from the band’s self-titled debut. Linnell had bad news: the setlist was too tight to make room for it. Mostly, he said, he was just worried about her arms. This is the kind of mercy They Might Be Giants offers: no song request granted, but sincere concern for your deltoids. Marty Beller during Shoehorn With Teeth. Photo: Alice Teeple The Johns. Photo: Alice Teeple By the time the band reached They’ll Need a Crane, Snowball in Hell (even acting out the samples from the album), and Ana Ng (half the front row busted out the choreography from the video), the show had built up the peculiar emotional math of that album: songs about failure, jobs, dread, love, geography, phonetics, power, small humiliations, and larger humiliations, all delivered with the zip of a novelty single and the aim of writers who can make a two-minute song feel like a trap sprung by a philosophy department. Ana Ng remains one of their perfect machines, sung by a room full of people who have probably spent half their lives knowing exactly how much of the world we want. (Answer: YOUR half!) The late-set curveballs kept the mood from slipping one inch. A cover of the Raspberries’ Overnight Sensation (Hit Record), Wu-Tang, stelluB, and monster hit Birdhouse in Your Soul closed the first half. Dan Miller. Photo: Alice Teeple Set Two opened with a magic trick:. Sapphire Bullets of Pure Love was recorded live entirely backwards, performed by the band like a stage full of Twin Peaks Giants, then played back in reverse for the audience. They had done this before, including at Kings Theatre in December 2024, but it remains a brilliant stunt, because the payoff is both technical and silly in the best possible sense. The crowd watches the process on screen, hears the garbled incantation, then gets the song snapped back into (mostly) recognizable shape. This go-around leaned hard into the breadth of their formidable catalogue, with a generous helping from Mink Car. Man, It’s So Loud in Here was a sleek little panic attack with a disco suit. Damn Good Times lived up to the boast without making a meal of it. Don’t Let’s Start still sounds like a nervous system trying to win an argument with itself. 2082 brought in later-career oddity with its own internal clock, while Wearing a Raincoat and Letterbox made room for the band’s softer zigzags. Danny Weinkauf. Photo: Alice Teeple This section also pulled me back to the strange pre-internet intimacy of Dial-A-Song, when fans could call a number printed in the albums and hear tinny little teasers through a phone line. Years before bands forced the same 30 seconds of music upon you in all forms of social media, years before the Information Superhighway itself, They Might Be Giants were already building a private broadcast system out of whatever was lying around. You could call a number, which still works today at (844) 387-6962. (Around the millennium, I remember hearing scratchy versions of Hovering Sombrero and Man, It’s So Loud In Here through that telephone haze (or was it the early website?), which made hearing the latter blasted out at Brooklyn Steel with horns and full-body force feel like a message from some absurd alternate future.) The horn section, by the way, nearly ran off with the show. Levine, Harrison, and Pender were wild, sharp, and loose in all the right places, turning songs that already had funny bones into strutting, brassy beasts. Dan Levine even brought out a euphonium, prompting the band to joke about how rarely one encounters such an instrument onstage. In another group, that might read as novelty. Here, it felt like proper policy. Of course, there would be a euphonium to go with Linnell’s accordion, “Main Squeeze!” Of course some kid in the audience is now doomed to ask for one at Guitar Center. (I should know, my first eBay purchase in 1999 was an accordion.) Dan Levine on euphonium and trombone. Photos: Alice Teeple Can’t Keep Johnny Down, Cloisonné, Twisting, and Dr. Worm gave the back half a terrific run, the band moving from cranky resilience to jazz-club surrealism to clean pop release. Dr. Worm in particular showed how much lift the larger band gives the material. The horns punched it upward, Beller drove it forward, and the Johns held court in the center of the commotion with wide grins. Dan Levine, Mark Pender and Stan Harrison. Photo: Alice Teeple Photo: Alice Teeple The encore was a brassy, batty victory lap. The Glamour of Rock led into Get Down, before Istanbul (Not Constantinople) gave the horn section another chance to go gloriously berserk. That Four Lads cover has been with the band so long that it belongs to them in the public imagination, and at Brooklyn Steel it sounded like a carnival contraption built by historians on espresso and bad sleep. Let Me Tell You About My Operation and When Will You Die kept the mood rude and ridiculous, and then came…as usual, The End of the Tour. Photo: Alice Teeple There was a glorious balance between discipline and derailment throughout the whole show. Boat of Car might have been denied (sorry, lady) – yet the night still felt full of trap doors, horns, jokes, props, backwards singing, rent memories, television references, and miniature explosions of odd grace. They Might Be Giants remain one of the rare bands who keep it delightfully genuine. Can’t wait until the next one…or at the very least, we’ll “meet at the end of the tour.” Catch them live next on the following dates this summer and fall: June 5 — Boston, MA — Citizens House of Blues Boston June 6 — Boston, MA — Citizens House of Blues Boston Sept. 24 — Milwaukee, WI — The Pabst Theater Sept. 25 — Milwaukee, WI — The Pabst Theater Sept. 26 — Madison, WI — Barrymore Theatre Sept. 27 — Madison, WI — Barrymore Theatre Sept. 29 — Kansas City, MO — The Truman Oct. 1 — Minneapolis, MN — First Avenue Oct. 2 — Minneapolis, MN — First Avenue Oct. 3 — St. Paul, MN — The Fitzgerald Theater Oct. 4 — St. Paul, MN — The Fitzgerald Theater Nov. 6 — Austin, TX — Emo’s Austin Nov. 7 — Austin, TX — Emo’s Austin Nov. 8 — Austin, TX — Emo’s Austin Nov. 10 — Houston, TX — The Heights Theater Nov. 11 — Houston, TX — The Heights Theater Nov. 13 — Dallas, TX — The Echo Lounge & Music Hall Nov. 14 — Dallas, TX — The Echo Lounge & Music Hall Nov. 19 — Washington, DC — 9:30 Club Nov. 20 — Washington, DC — 9:30 Club Nov. 21 — Washington, DC — 9:30 Club Nov. 22 — Washington, DC — 9:30 Club Follow They Might Be Giants: Website Instagram Facebook YouTube Spotify Dan Miller. Photo: Alice Teeple John Flansburgh. Photo: Alice Teeple Mark Pender and Stan Harrison. Photo: Alice Teeple John Linnell. items.body: In this recording by bassist, composer and bandleader Ben Wolfe, titled Any Time After Now, there is a quiet assurance, with nothing straining for effect or feeling manufactured. Recorded in a single studio day alongside vibraphonist Joel Ross, pianist Sullivan Fortner, tenor saxophonist Chris Lewis and drummer Aaron Kimmel, the album spans ten tracks of original Wolfe compositions and exhibits a natural cohesion that reflects musicians deeply attuned to one another. The opener, "Any Time After Now," swings with effortless authority. Wolfe's bass lines move with confidence beneath Lewis and Ross's contributions, while Fortner brings a strong rhythmic sense to the tune. Kimmel takes an imaginative turn on his kit, adding to the bebop narrative. "Waltz II" is striking for its delicacy. Buoyed by Wolfe's deep tone and steady beat, Ross and Fortner interact with arresting sensitivity, each phrase answered by the other. "Blues" evokes a hazy, after-hours atmosphere. Lewis delivers an expressive performance, smoky, relaxed, and soulful. Ross follows with an improvisation rich in harmonic nuance, and Fortner settles into a blues statement grounded in groove and touch. "5/4 Groove" unfolds as Kimmel shapes the asymmetrical pulse with ease, while Fortner crafts an extended meditation brimming with momentum and tension. Wolfe's solo is a highlight, lyrical, poised, and deeply musical. Wolfe, an unusual musician who associates music with color, shape and texture, writes compositions that carry visual weight. The music shifts between shadows, light, density and openness with remarkable fluidity. The result is a performance in which the band knows exactly how to inhabit these spaces. "Down with Gravity" brings sharp angles and earthy funk. Wolfe and Kimmel work hand in glove, while Lewis stretches out with a harmonic vocabulary that yields clarity of ideas. There is a real bite here without sacrificing sophistication. "Always Four" opens with an assertive flourish from Kimmel, then settles into tightly focused exchanges between Ross and Fortner. Kimmel is back on board with crisp playing, taking the tune out as each idea feels purposeful. "Til The Next Time" is a silky bossa nova that glides effortlessly into the ear. Ross, in full vibrato, phrases beautifully over Wolfe's subtle plucking. Fortner and Kimmel keep everything light and pleasant. The closing bonus track, "Green," swings with optimism and zest. Ross and Fortner carry the instrumental load with a keen sense of musical drama, while Wolfe and Kimmel deliver sharply etched pulses. The number offers a clear picture of Wolfe's melodic, thoughtful, and generous compositional voice.
items._cn_summary: 贝斯手兼作曲家Ben Wolfe领衔的五重奏专辑，以原声爵士为核心框架，涵盖bebop、华尔兹、布鲁斯、波萨诺瓦、放克等多种传统爵士语汇。乐队编制包括颤音琴、钢琴、次中音萨克斯、贝斯和鼓，整体呈现自然流畅的室内乐质感。Wolfe的创作理念颇具个人特色，他将音乐与色彩、形状、质感等视觉意象关联，作品在不同情绪空间间游走。然而，该专辑整体仍属当代主流后波普爵士范畴，演奏技法和结构编排均在传统框架内，未涉及自由即兴、电子声响、跨界融合等实验性元素。节奏与和声处理稳健扎实，乐手互动默契，但缺乏突破性的声音探索和前卫美学，与偏向实验与即兴路线的听者期待存在较大距离。

items.body: Storybook: The Music Of Mark Miller is at one level the unfolding narrative of its 10 musical selections. At another, it is a tale about its primary author, Mark Miller, who traced his journey from {jny: Racine}} to New York City with his previous release Mark Miller: The Return Of Slide Huxtable (Slide Huxtable, 2008)—a long road that is a serious jazz player's dream of making it in the Big Apple. But most of all, it is a compelling reminder to listeners everywhere that the Manhattan jazz experience is incomplete without a trip to hear the Birdland Big Band. Birdland's original, long defunct basement club at "The Jazz Corner of the World" (Broadway and 52nd) now occupies a bigger mid-town area, bounded on the north by Jazz at Lincoln Center (60 St.) and, on the south, by the "new" Birdland (44th St). Start at 52nd St., walk 8 blocks in either direction, and you are there. But which direction? Is there a significant difference? Some observers have suggested that big band music from the north references the genius of Duke Ellington, whereas the sounds to the south are aligned with the swing of Count Basie. Yet "Storybook," the eponymous title of the album's Grammy-nominated first track, sounds like something else entirely. Miller—much of whose "schooling" was on the road as trombonist-composer with the Minneapolis-based jazz group, The Motion Poets—has constructed a brilliant sonic gateway that owes as much to Bach and Bartok as to Ellington or Count Basie. Starting with a stately 3-note descending motif, the composition builds on that figure with rich harmonies and vibrant dynamics, answered by an ascending counter-melody played by the lower brass. Soon, the entire sequence is repeated, with the addition of creative commentary from Brandon Lee's flugelhorn. After a sharply articulated, vigorously syncopated version of the primary motif, Kenny Barron's infectious "Water Lily." Unlike earlier recorded versions that are slower and light-spirited, the tune here is taken at a driving tempo with accompaniment by piano and drums that borders on the intrusive (likely due to an over-hot audio mix-down). Besides an inventive piano solo by Kenny Ascher, the piece showcases the commanding artistry of saxophonist Troy Roberts, whose closing cadenza balances impressive pyrotechnics with satisfying musical taste. Next, the standard, "Tenderly," lightens the mood with a sprightly version of a waltz that, with the notable exception of Bill Evans' up-tempo version, usually receives the slow, pensive reading of Rosemary Clooney or the even slower 4/4 versions by Sara Vaughn and Billie Holiday. Miller's arrangement exhibits remarkable attention to detail, replete with spiraling flutes that simulate butterflies to complement the spring setting for vocalist Nicole Zuraitis. Brief solos by Sam Dillon (a. sax) and Raul Agraz (trpt) fit seamlessly with the colorful seasonal mix. Miller's own "Chorale and Alleluia" is as contemplative and celebratory as its title might suggest. It features the percussive thunder of Chris Smith, who will also be critical to the driving samba rhythm of Chick Corea's "Spain." Tom Harrell's "Sail Away" is an inviting melody launched without affectation by Glenn Drewes' reassuring flugel. After band director David DeJesus' soprano sax has taken control of the cruise, Drews resumes his storytelling by, in effect, shutting off the engine (i.e., piano, bass, drums) and allowing only the sounds of wind and water for several choruses—the pulse of the band sans rhythm section. It is tempting to continue with a play-by-play analysis if only to identify the soloists in an ensemble with no weak links. The Birdland Band is "deep" with talent, each player capable of assuming solo duties on any given night. Take, for example, "WTF," in which trombonist/composer Miller resumes the cruise with a witty trombone exchange between James Burton III and Sara Jacovino, one that recalls the musical conversations by J.J. Johnson and Jay and Kai Winding. The last third of the program is cued up by the standard "Close Your Eyes," which opens with Zuraitis close to the mic as she fashions a soft, pitch-perfect, improvised chorus before yielding to an Ascher piano solo that swings with the sure-fingered authority of Wynton Kelly. Following a good-humored, equally swinging turn by bass trombonist, James Borowski, Zuraitis re-enters for an "out" chorus that soon becomes "far-out," her voice rising in pitch and volume to the level of a Maynard Ferguson set-closer. It works because the vocalist implants herself in the trumpet section, rising to a powerful climax as the job requires. Finally, we receive a healthy reminder that "swing" does not require a thing except a ride cymbal and a hi-hat. (If only audio engineers could figure out a way to include the shimmer of a Zildjian in their mastering of live sounds.) Rodrigo de Arunez's "Concierto" and Corea's "Spain" are worthy additions to those already in print. And they are among the most "honest," avoiding orchestral instruments (French horns, double reeds, tympani, etc.) as well as electronic devices (Fender Rhodes, phaser boxes, onboard modulating effects). The result is a focus that remains fixed on the music, not the gear. And then there is the memorable close-out for "Spain"—an ascending Miller bass-line that, in effect, resolves a sparking, fractious debate between big band and drums, then between sections within the ensemble. "The DoubleDown," the last track of the regular program, evokes a Sunday night gospel meeting with its inviting singalong melody in ¾. The primary preacher is Ron Wilkins, whose testifying on plunger-muted trombone produces a meditative bass solo by Noriko Ueda. But rather than exit quietly, the congregation is led back by saxophones to the main theme, then a sudden stop and lift to a new key for a final testament by Mark Miller's emphatic postlude on trombone. Church is out, but the congregation's spirits crave more action. "Nonsense," an original shuffle-rhythm blues composed by Miller and Zuraitis, answers the need to sustain the sense of play embedded in every true storybook. Zuraitis delivers a nonsensical lyric in the strongest musical terms, conversing over stop-time chords with Miller's and Wilkins' vocal trombones. Next, she handles "vocalese" lines in tight unison with tricky instrumental figures. Finally, there is a vocal exchange, over pedal-tone bass, between the entire band and its girl singer, who has the last word: "Nonsense? Come on, whatever gets you. Small wonder that, after hearing a call like that, visitors are setting aside Friday nights for a return to Birdland.
items._cn_summary: The Birdland Big Band的《Storybook》是一张以Mark Miller原创作品为核心的当代大乐队爵士专辑。Miller的作曲受到巴赫与巴托克的影响，标题曲以三音下行动机展开，融合对位手法与丰富的和声层次，展现出一定的古典对位思维与大乐队配器功底。专辑也收录Kenny Barron的《Water Lily》与经典曲目《Tenderly》等，编排注重细节，如长笛模拟蝴蝶的音型设计体现了一定的画面感与叙事意图。整体而言，这是一张编曲扎实、演奏严谨的当代大乐队爵士作品，融合了古典作曲技法与传统大乐队摇摆美学，但在实验性、即兴自由度与声响探索方面较为保守，与学院派自由爵士、前卫即兴或电子跨界等更具冒险精神的方向存在明显距离。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — My gawsh, there are three bands named DERIVA in Spain! One was a Basque rock band formed in 2001from Donostia-San Sebasti�n, another post-metal band from Madrid that released one album in 2016 andthen finally the subject of this review, an all-instrumental mostly solo project of guitarist /bassist / drum programmer Javier Hern�ndez from Soria in Castilla y Le�n. Hernandez played invarious bands including Sol Negro and Pangea before finally setting some of his pent up ideas freeon this project with guitarist Carlos Rubio along for the ride. Rubio played in some of the samebands in the future. This DERIVA project has so far only released a single album titled ECLEPSYSwhich came out in 2012 and showcases these two seasoned musicians cranking out 16 tracks ofinstrumental prog metal.Pretty much an album out of the Joe Satriani type of guitar savvy hard rock and progressive metalinstrumental playbook, this album finds the two guitarists delivering melodic riffs and solos alongwith only a bass and programmed drums but despite the lack of players involved here actually comesoff pretty dynamically delivered with a series of strong tracks that navigate various techniques,exotic mood settings and rhythmic formats. A few touches of keyboards offer the occasionalatmospheric presence but for the most part this is a brawling dudes only jamfest where two guitarsduke it out while keeping their eyes on the melodic prize. The duo play together seamlessly and mostsurprisingly the drums actually sound fairly real. The production is also top notch which adds tothe squeaky clean feel of the album.The opening "Estrella del este" sets a strong tone with a mystique of the Middle East findingthrashing stomping power chords with ethnic flavors reminding me a bit of the Australian band BaKonly sans the vocal charm. "Life Groove" jumps into more progressive territory while "Babel" offersa bit of alt metal flavor. A few ballads enter the scene with tracks like "Es Por Ti" offeringslower clean guitar sounds mixed with crunchy leads which in this case reminds me of some of thoseho hum Pikes from Buckethead that never seem to end. While the duo never runs out of steam as far astheir playing abilities are concerned, the album does suffer from too much of a good thing withoutany true break from the same formula strewn out in different melodic motifs. More stylistic shiftsand tone changes would've gone a long way towards making this lengthy release less monotonous by thetime the end nears. "Moonster" is a nice change with echoey twangy guitar tones and escapes themetal vibe altogether.Overall this is one of those fairly competent examples of a musicians stockpile of ideas coming tofruition in one chock-filled display of opportunities finally realized. All in all it's acaptivating album that delivers on all fronts and for what it is, it's really a great album howeverthere isn't really anything new under the sun as albums like this were being cranked out as far backas the 1980s so there has been no shortage of similar minded guitarists releasing such examples eversince. These two dudes do a great job with the limited resources they are presenting and given thatit's basically two guitars, a bass and drum program it's well done however it's not one of thosealbums that will make you feel like breaking the bank to run out and get. For one thing i keepwishing the two would break into more daring metal diversity but that never really happens. By thetime the album ends it sounds like a retread of everything that came before which is more likelythan not given no vocalist on board to distract from what sounds more like background music to lyricoriented songs. Good but not great.

items.body: Picture this: Having assembled a supporting cast, finalized the playlist and booked a studio, you are ready to make the debut recording as leader of your own ensemble, only to learn that, hours earlier, said studio in East Lansing, Michigan, had been devastated by a tornado. That is exactly what happened to trombonist Eli Howell in May 2025. Fortunately, thanks to some quick thinking and deft maneuvering by album producer Michael Dease and others, a room was found at Howell's alma mater, Michigan State University, and the recording session went on as planned, without the usual isolation or overdubs, thus providing the sort of immediacy that was the norm in early-day studio sessions. It was not the first time that Howell had faced and overcome adversity. In 2023, he was diagnosed with focal dystonia, a neurological movement disorder that forced him to stop playing trombone for a year. Once past that, he saddled up again and was looking forward to recording with his sextet when the studio abruptly disappeared. Undaunted, Howell and his companions changed the location and started anew. The result of their efforts is a rather mixed bag whose several highlights serve to overshadow those moments that are less engaging. The session shines brightest on the standard "Alone Together," bassist Rodney Whitaker's well-grooved "For Garrison," Howell's high-stepping "One for Steve" (for fellow trombonist Steve Davis), the graceful "Dear Helen" (written for his great-grandmother), and Raul De Souza's rollicking finale, "A Vontade Mesmo." Howell's valve trombone duel with Dease on "A Vontade Mesmo" is especially impressive, as are Sharel Cassity's exquisite flute work on "One for Helen" and the snug group dynamics on "Alone Together" and "One for Steve," with incisive solos by Howell, Cassity, Whitaker, pianist Xavier Davis and trumpeter Brian Lynch, an added bonus. There were two recording sessions, three days apart, with alto saxophonist Thomas Noble, pianist Miki Hayama, bassist Langston Kitchen and drummer Colleen Clark replacing the core group on "A Clear Day" and "A Vontade Mesmo." Trombonist Wycliffe Gordon makes a guest appearance on his composition "I Remember Al" (a tribute to the late trombonist Al Grey), trying his best (and largely succeeding) with voice, mutes and other effects to make the trombone sound like anything but a trombone. Howell shares center stage with Lynch and alto Cassity on the album's nimble opening number, Jerry Bock and Sheldon Harnick's "Matchmaker," from the Broadway musical Fiddler on the Roof. As noted, an album whose high points readily outweigh any lesser moments, and one that is definitely worth your time and consideration.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是长号手Eli Howell领衔的六重奏传统主流爵士录音，作品涵盖爵士标准曲如《Alone Together》《Matchmaker》以及原创曲目，整体风格属于学院派后波普范畴。专辑在密歇根州录制，因龙卷风破坏原定录音室而临时转至密歇根州立大学完成，采用不隔音、无叠录的早期录音方式，具有一定的现场即时性。乐手阵容包括Brian Lynch、Wycliffe Gordon、Sharel Cassity、Rodney Whitaker等爵士乐坛中坚力量，演奏功底扎实。然而乐评坦承整张专辑是'好坏参半'的混合体，部分段落存在吸引力不足的问题。音乐风格偏向传统主流爵士，缺乏实验性、前卫性或跨领域融合元素，与用户偏好的实验、前卫、自由即兴、电子或世界音乐方向相距甚远。

items.body:
Secretly Group has joined in partnership with Music Declares Emergency and the Music Climate Pact to mark World Environment Day 2026 by releasing a number of special edition releases on 100% reclaimed vinyl material.

"Bon Iver’s debut full-length For Emma, Forever Ago made major waves in critics’ circles based on the strength of an early artist-pressed advance CD and a couple awe-inspiring sets at CMJ back in October 2007. 

Bon Iver (pronounced: bohn eevair; French for “good winter” and spelled wrong on purpose) is a greeting, a celebration and a sentiment. It is a new statement of an artist moving on and establishing the groundwork for a lasting career.

For Emma, Forever Ago is the debut of this lineage of songs. As a whole, the record is entirely cohesive throughout and remains centered around a particular aesthetic, prompted by the time and place for which it was recorded. Justin Vernon, the primary force behind Bon Iver, seems to have tested his boundaries to the maximum, and in doing so has managed to break free from any pre-cursing or finished forms. It wasn’t planned. The goal was to hibernate. Vernon moved to a remote cabin in the woods of Northwestern Wisconsin at the onset of winter. He lived there alone for three months, filling his days with wood splitting and other chores around the land. This solitary time slowly began feeding a bold, uninhibited new musical focus. The days slowly evolved into nights filled with twelve-hour recording blocks, breaking only for trips on the tractor into the pines to saw and haul firewood, or for frozen sunrises high up a deer stand. All of his personal trouble, lack of perspective, heartache, longing, love, loss and guilt that had been stock piled over the course of the past six years, was suddenly purged into the form of song."
items._cn_summary: 本文围绕Bon Iver首张专辑《For Emma, Forever Ago》的环保再版展开，着重描述了主创Justin Vernon在威斯康星州偏远木屋中独自生活三个月后完成录制的创作背景，提及了专辑的情感来源与生活状态。这张作品本质上是独立民谣，以原声吉他和人声为核心，音乐手法偏向传统民谣创作范畴，未涉及实验声响设计、电子元素或爵士即兴，与实验/前卫/电子/暗潮等偏好类型距离较远。专辑具有一定的个人化美学和情感真实性，但跨类型融合度极低。评论本身更偏向作品背景介绍与再版宣传信息，缺乏对音乐本体深入的分析与评论。整体定位为广受评论界认可的独立民谣经典，在主流独立音乐版图中具有重要地位，但与用户偏好的前卫实验路线吻合度有限。

items.body:
Moroder-esque disco kosmiche by a South Korean artist taking her debut bow on Mule Musiq after turns on Prins Thomas’ Internasjonal and her own Uju Records.

Time for a bit of pure Euro-disco peacockery with ‘Starlight Arcade’, riding a wave of late ‘70s/early ‘80s disco élan with coolly poised reserve and sleek horsepower where it matters. It may take a well educated ear to draw a line between Shubostar’s sound and the OGs, such is her sophisticated club finesse.

All four cuts are built to please in a time-honoured style, smoothly shifting thru the gears from the chromatic star dust melody and insistent canter of ‘Abbiamo’, thru the punchy drums and arcing hero synth spumes of ‘Gamgi’ ripened for Adonis posing on the ‘floor, thru the subtly darker edge and stride of ‘Starlight Arcade’ to a modal swag hinting at early new beat inspirations on ‘Tip Top’.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以欧式迪斯科和宇宙迪斯科为基调的舞曲专辑，由韩国艺术家制作，在独立厂牌Mule Musiq发行。音乐风格延续了七十年代末至八十年代初迪斯科的华丽质感，融合了Moroder式的合成器律动与少量新节拍元素。整体制作精良，俱乐部导向明显，四首作品各自具备不同的情绪层次与节奏走向。然而，该作品本质上属于复古迪斯科舞曲范畴，在实验性、前卫性、声响设计创新等方面较为有限，更接近对经典的精致复刻而非突破性创作。对于偏好实验电子、IDM、氛围音乐、前卫爵士或暗潮工业的听众而言，这张专辑的契合度较低。韩国艺术家的身份为作品带来一定地域新鲜感，但音乐本身的风格定位并未充分体现非西方文化的独特视角。

items.excerpt: Carolina Chocolate Drops - Genuine Negro Jig / a RootsWorld review
items.body: A little before the end of the last century, a revelatory compilation appeared, seemingly from nowhere. From Where I Stand: The Black Experience In Country Music opened a window on something so many didn’t even know existed to show that country music had never been a white preserve. That album was a few years before the Carolina Chocolate Drops burst on the scene, reclaiming the Black heritage in country and string band music, plus a great deal more. Genuine Negro Jig , their third release, saw them move up to the prestigious Nonesuch label, a powerful artistic imprimatur, winning them a Grammy for an album very far removed from the mainstream. Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops This expanded 15th anniversary edition marks a good time to look back at the band’s mix of Piedmont string band and traditional music, nestling beside early 20th century blues, and a few original and modern pieces in the mix (like the Tom Waits-penned “Trampled Rose”). The trio roared into the music, playing it with fire and unalloyed joy – yet also with plenty of subtlety; list to “Snowden’s Jig (Genuine Negro Jig)” for a taste of how the members worked together. For many, this would have been the first opportunity to hear Rhiannon Giddens – quite a big global star these days – and Don Flemons, as well as Sule Greg Wilson, standard bears for an idea whose time had come. This is an album very much worth of this deluxe reissue treatment, a real landmark, not simply for the career of the Carolina Chocolate Drops, but for roots music in general. And people responded – hence that Grammy. Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops There are plenty of bonus tracks here, all worth hearing, but the real meat is on the original release. There’s the delicious, sultry blues of “Why Don’t You Do Right?”, the wild string band abandon of “Cindy Gal,” Giddens’s unaccompanied voice on “Reynardine,” and the full-tilt race through “Sandy Boys.” It’s exhilarating, but so much more. There’s deep thought given to the arrangements and the interplay between instruments and voices. Genuine Negro Jig (15th Anniversary Edition) by Carolina Chocolate Drops The band aren’t purists. They don’t need to be. Whatever the sources for the material, they transform it and turn it into something that speaks with their voice. Released a decade after From Where I Stand , Genuine Negro Jig was a bold manifesto that still speaks loudly today. It is an album very much worth of this deluxe reissue, waiting for a new audience to discover.
items._cn_summary: Carolina Chocolate Drops的《Genuine Negro Jig》是一张以皮埃蒙特弦乐队传统为核心的美国根源音乐专辑，融合了早期二十世纪蓝调、民谣弦乐以及少量原创和现代作品。专辑在文化层面具有重要意义，致力于重新发掘黑人在乡村与弦乐传统中的遗产地位，Rhiannon Giddens等人的演绎充满活力与技巧。音乐风格属于美国传统民间音乐范畴，编曲扎实但缺乏实验性声响设计或前卫元素，与实验、前卫、爵士、电子等方向的关联较弱。尽管存在一定的跨文化与传承价值，但整体风格更接近传统民谣而非用户偏好的世界融合或实验领域，且发行厂牌Nonesuch隶属华纳旗下，具有一定主流属性。

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter’s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages – and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: “Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.” Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It’s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he’s selected some great talent to help – guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like “Sam Bamford” and “Mary Fildes,” while the three short pieces that comprise “The Monkey Rides The Mare” capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It’s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time.
items._cn_summary: Sean Cooney（Young'Uns成员）创作的概念专辑，以1819年彼得卢屠杀事件为题材，结合兰开夏工业民谣传统。专辑以书籍形式呈现，配以历史信件、政治漫画与插图，是一次多媒体叙事尝试。音乐风格为英式传统民谣，邀请Eliza Carthy、Sam Carter、Jennifer Reid等民谣音乐人参与，以原声吉他、小提琴等传统乐器为主。歌曲围绕历史事件展开，捕捉集会期待、骑兵冲击的恐怖与事后悲怆，聚焦Sam Bamford、Mary Fildes等个人视角叙事。三位歌手的声线构成核心张力，小编制组合制造出强劲声场。整体属于英伦传统民谣范畴，具有一定的历史文化叙事价值，但缺乏实验性声响设计或跨类型融合元素。

items.excerpt: Tiny Sun (Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke) - Vanishment
items.body: Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar. Vanishment contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina’s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice. The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette. Kerosene Madrigal The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, “Kerosene Madrigal,” is a sort of miner’s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of “Imagined Love” reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy “Don’t Fault the Stars for Falling” could have been a Dolly Parton tune. A Grand Expanse “A Grand Expanse” has a more ambitious arrangement. It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun. The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it. Berceuse Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto’s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以美式民谣为核心的专辑，由三位来自不同音乐背景的创作者合作完成，风格涵盖布鲁斯、乡村和独立民谣等元素。专辑收录十八首短小的作品，编曲简洁克制，以原声吉他、尤克里里、滑棒吉他和键盘为主，人声清澈高亢。歌词围绕失去、放弃和宿命感展开，整体氛围被描述为带有梦境感的音乐。三位成员各自有流行电子、根源音乐和影视配乐的背景，但成品仍偏向传统的美式民谣路线。对于关注实验、前卫、爵士、电子或暗潮的听众来说，这张专辑在风格上距离较远，但其中精炼的短曲形式和跨领域合作的特质使其具备一定的艺术品质。

Signalling their signing to Fire Records, Bad Bunch is scheduled for release on a currently unannounced date later this year. Their last LP, Electric Brick Wall, came out on Drag City in 2014. items.body: Growing up in the Chicago area with Jamaican heritage running deep, Kazayah came to roots reggae as a calling. Her latest single “Mustard Seed” pairs her with Tikur Anbessa Records, the Los Angeles label run by Fikir Amlak, a singer, multi-instrumentalist and producer with 20 years in the business, and London’s King Alpha, a Ghanaian-born, West London producer and sound system operator who has spent years pressing dub and roots riddims to vinyl and taking them to sound system stages across Europe and beyond. Amlak and King Alpha have worked together since 2014, giving the record a production backbone with a decade of roots credibility behind it. The track rides a heavy steppas riddim, deep bassline and crisp percussion giving her warm, focused delivery the room to push the message forward. In both biblical and Rastafari tradition the mustard seed is faith that grows from almost nothing, and for an artist who found Rastafari as a reckoning with Black identity and cultural pride, that image runs through everything she makes, placing her in the line of Marcia Griffiths and Jah9. Stream “Mustard Seed” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Kazayah – Mustard Seed appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: Kazayah的《Mustard Seed》是一首传统根基雷鬼单曲，融合了沉重的steppas riddim律动、深沉贝斯线和清脆打击乐。她拥有牙买加血统，在芝加哥成长，与洛杉矶独立厂牌Tikur Anbessa Records和伦敦制作人King Alpha合作。歌词主题围绕拉斯塔法里信仰与黑人文化身份认同展开，风格上被比作Marcia Griffiths和Jah9。整体制作属于正统的根源雷鬼范式，着重于信息传递和律动感，在声响实验和电子元素方面几乎没有探索。对于偏好实验、前卫、爵士即兴和电子声响的听众而言，这首作品显得传统而保守，缺少突破性的跨界融合或声音设计上的创新。

items.body: Review by FalconBleck — #59 ReviewI found this one because of a certain vocalist from another prog rock band that I love, any recentsurprise is welcome, I'm sure that I haven't heard everything in the Genesis world, is just that Istruggle finding new things to hear, and this was and is what I needed.- Watcher Of The Skies (Hush): Already an interesting proposal with a different sound, then adifferent introduction that starts with the chords, and then the main riff in acoustic guitar soundsgreat, then in familiar territory, but still very modern, it works really good for a new version ofthe song, no complaints, I'm sure that I come back to this version from time to time, well doneHush.- Firth Of Fifth (Over The Garden Wall): Very similar to the original, barely any difference, doneas faithful as it can be, as much as I like how it sounds, I sometimes feel like I would ratherlisten to the original, since they are so similar, but at the same time, they are so similar thatthis version can satisfy me from listening to the original. There are subtle differences, thekeyboard middle part is done with an acoustic guitar, at least the main part, then it goes back tokeyboard, it sounds great, but again, so similar, honestly well done, the quality on this album hasbeen great so far. Ok, people want to know about the guitar solo, some people only seem to careabout that, I get it, its great, but there's more song to be enjoyed, anyways, the solo is like amix between Steve and Daryl, that's also great, a very well done Firth Of Fifth.- Undertow (Jay Tausig): Continuing with quality and versions being very similar, this one is reallyclose again, however, this one sounds a bit more melancholic, the voice has less power than Phil,its like closer to Tony Banks, and he made the song, add to this the faded keyboards, and you have aversion that feels more melancholic. The piano sound is also more up-front, I keep coming back tothis version for those slight differences.- Ripples (Annie Haslam): I found this album through this song, the vocalist of Renaissance playinga Genesis song? I have to listen to this, and then I found that it was Ripples, least to say myexpectations were very high. Then I heard it, and at first it was everything I expected, she doesher own spin into the song and sounds great, however, no solo, instead a more happy version of thesong, that I kind of dig, but at the same time, I would like to hear Annie singing over the originalinstrumental done by Genesis, at least this is the closest we can get.- Back in NYC (Kevin Gilbert): Kind of prophetic in a way, Genesis did a lighter version of TheLamb, and this one starts like that, then it obviously goes back to being the usual song, there wasmaybe a need for this to be 2 versions, but it doesn't matter, the song introduces some new ideas,the quiet parts are more quiet, and sometimes even funky, it really plays more with thejuxtaposition of moods that the original song introduces, and while I like the vocals and what's inhere, I still want to listen to the original more, and the ending with the NYC atmosphere issomething I truly don't like, just stop the song beforethat comes.- For Absent Friends (Richard Sinclair): I really admire this version of the song, the vocals areendearing, the instrumentation feels richer with the added strings and harpsichord, and if thatwasn't enough, the song gets extended to almost twice its length, this is definitely a must listenfrom this album. - Mama (Magellan): I like how the drum pattern sounds, most of it gets respected, however, I'm notsure about the rest of the sounds, for a moment the song is just fine, the introduction is fast,which is nice, but then the first laugh gets ruined by an uninspired drum roll, the voice justdoesn't get there, for some reason the notes are all high as soon as possible, it just doesn't work,its as if they wanted to be louder than the original just for the sake of it. Finally we reach thelaugh, and again, its too much, the point of the song is that it was simple and tense, if you wantedto add more into the song, it would've been a good idea to hear the pre-release version, however, itwasn't released back then yet. I will just say, for a moment it was very promising, production isgood, I have no doubt that these are good musicians, just obviously not Genesis.- Man Of Our Times (Enchant): I usually don't mention production, because my copy of the CD could bethe problem, well, I'm listening from YT, and this one sounds weak for some reason, like its lackingsomething, but that's probably the upload, ignoring all that, this version is very comparable to theoriginal, except for everything that sounds a bit weaker, the strongs are the over-drive guitar andthe background voices that sound louder than in the original, that also do a more noticeablefun stereo play, which is a production win. Honestly, this version is fine, but I would ratherlisten to the original, there's nothing that makes me comeback to this version because its sosimilar, the over-drive doesn't convince me.- Many Too Many (Peter Bardens): One advantage this version has over the original is that the firstincrease is more subtle, and the second is bigger, while in the original both feel similar, however,the original has a very cool guitar solo that's heavily reduced in this version, that could've beena very neat improvement.- Entangled (Shadow Gallery): Incredibly similar to the original, well done instrumental, the voiceson the chorus though sound like the three musketeers, it doesn't work and it takes me away from thesong. The guitars sound very clean and pleasant, the ending is not as strong, yet very close,overall a good version that feels new, it just needs to fix the chorus. Minus points for the fade-out instead of having an ending.- Squonk (Cairopaiva): There are some decisions I don't like, the instruments seem to alternatebetween ideas that don't work well, they add things that could be welcome, but they aren't cleverenough, they feel out of place, the guitar at the start, the drums a bit after that, the best thingabout this song is the voice, the vocalist does a very good job, sounds fresh and respectful, hefits the song well enough, which is surprising by how difficult it is. The ending is ruined here,why do you have talking, and a very early fade-out? Terrible decision.- I Know What I Like (Crack The Sky): What is this? Crack The Sky? They are great, but what was theidea here? Being different just for the sake of it? It doesn't fit the rest of this album as well,its so weird, but I kind of dig the style change, it sounds more scary than happy, I think that'ssomething good, but other than that, this is just a curiosity, they managed something veryinteresting here, it doesn't sound like anything on this album, or Crack The Sky, or any decisionthat Genesis would've taken with this song, but it still sounds a bit like Genesis, its so weird.- The Carpet Crawlers (Michael Zentner): I'm sorry, the voice doesn't do it for me, its too forced,the kind of forced voice you get away with in high school, like no one told you that it wasn't good.This is sadly one of worst Carpet Crawlers I have heard so far, I'm sorry for being so harsh, Ireally don't like it, the drums are too loud an static, the strings are barely here and I completelymiss the keyboard I love so much, the guitar is fine, but not enough... This is definitely a CarpetCrawlers, but its just so under-cooked, and the single voice is over-done, totally missing the pointof the song. The best I can say that it seems to be a respectful attempt, although the forced voicefeels like a mockery at times, I just can't recommend this one.- Keep It Dark (World Trade): Now this one is weaker, but it respects even the smallest details atthe best it can, however, it really lacks an stronger bass and keyboards, the voice is fine,obviously not Phil, but its well done. The differences are so small that they barely matter, andalso the song ends faster, well done but not enough.In conclusion, this album is a bit of a mix bag, there are some interesting proposals and even someideas that can be good to listen as a new version that compliments the original, however, I don'tthink that any of these versions represent the best of what this artists can do, I appreciate theeffort a lot and the amount of Genesis eras that they covered, I'm glad that this exists, I justwish that it was better and that it had a better name, because some of what's in here needs to beheard by Genesis and prog rock fans.

items.body: Russian punk collective Pussy Riot announced “CYKA,” their debut full-length album, scheduled for release on June 12, 2026, on digital streaming platforms. The fourteen-track record compresses fourteen years of the group’s activity – including protest actions, imprisonment and exile – into a single body of work. The album title translates from Russian as “bitch.” Lead single “Candy Dopamine,” featuring Avenged Sevenfold, is out now with an official music video on YouTube. “Candy Dopamine” was co-written by Pussy Riot with Avenged Sevenfold vocalist M. Shadows and guitarist Zacky Vengeance. The track mixes pop with alternative rock and features guest vocals from M. Shadows alongside heavy guitar work. Pussy Riot founder Nadya Tolokonnikova described the song as a statement on prescription and designer drug culture: “It started with my dependence on antidepressants, but it’s also looking at everyone now, mentalhealthmaxxing and looksmaxxing via pills and injections. It’s not a judgment, it’s just an observation, and my personal experience with these things is that I have to be in a long-term relationship with them for my PTSD and depression.” This is the second collaboration between Avenged Sevenfold and Pussy Riot. In 2023, Tolokonnikova appeared on a reworked version of the Avenged Sevenfold track “We Love You,” re-released as “We Love You Moar,” raising awareness of the situation of LGBTQ+ people in Russia. The album’s earlier single “Disobey” was released in May 2026. Its music video consists of footage from Pussy Riot’s “Storm of Venice” protest action at the 61st Venice Biennale, in which more than fifty members of the collective stormed the Russian pavilion with clouds of pink smoke. Ukrainian activist group FEMEN joined the demonstration, which was staged in protest at Russia’s return to the international art event. The 90-second track features distorted guitars, shouted vocals and chants of “disobey,” with lyrics in English and Russian condemning fascism and political silence. ‘CYKA’: collaborators, tracklist, and Putin challenge Other confirmed contributors on “CYKA” include B-Real of Cypress Hill (on the track “Gore”) and singer-songwriter Salem Ilese (on “Utopia”). Russian President Vladimir Putin is listed as a contributor on the self-titled track “Cyka.” Tolokonnikova adds: “I’m not gonna give him royalties though, they can add it to my list of crimes.” Tolokonnikova also announced a public challenge to Putin to fight her at the UFC Freedom 250 event, scheduled for June 14 at the White House. In her statement, she says: “All these old men ruining the world right now act tough, but we see through their fragile egos, and I’m not afraid to call them out. I challenge President Putin to a cage match. He loses? He gets the fuck out of Ukraine.” About Pussy Riot Pussy Riot is a Russian punk and protest collective founded in Moscow in 2011. The group operates as a loose, rotating collective but is closely associated with founders Nadya Tolokonnikova (also known as Nadya Tolokno) and Maria Alyokhina (known as Masha). The group staged performances in public spaces across Moscow as acts of political protest, often wearing brightly colored balaclavas. In February 2012, three members – Tolokonnikova, Alyokhina and Yekaterina Samutsevich – were arrested following a performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. They were convicted of “hooliganism motivated by religious hatred” and sentenced to two years in a penal colony. Samutsevich was released on appeal in October 2012; Tolokonnikova and Alyokhina served their full sentences, released in December 2013. The trial attracted international attention. Following their release, Tolokonnikova and Alyokhina continued their political activism and released music under the Pussy Riot name. The group collaborated with Boys Noize on “Rage” in 2021, and with Boyfriend on the electropop single “Dance With the Devil” in 2023. In July 2025, a new Russian law criminalized searching for Pussy Riot content online. In April 2026, Tolokonnikova was formally indicted by Russia’s Investigative Committee for alleged violations of the country’s “foreign agent” law. “CYKA” is Pussy Riot’s debut full-length album. It is released June 12, 2026.

items.body:
Since everyone else has written something about the centennials of Miles Davis and John Coltrane, why not join the parade? It is a good opportunity to look at the timeline of bassists the legendary trumpeter and saxophonist used. Born just under four months apart, the pair worked together under the elder Davis' name periodically between Fall 1955 and Spring 1957 before a more steady affiliation in 1958-1960.

It is in that latter period that this analysis will begin, as it gives a convenient bit of serendipity: the fact that two of the their most famed albums were made in that period, Davis' Kind Blue (March 2nd and April 22nd, 1959 for Columbia) and Coltrane's Giant Steps (May 4th-5th and December 2nd, 1959). And the analysis will end with Coltrane's death in 1967, which came during the tenure of Davis' "second great quintet" and before his groups swelled and electrified during his fusion period.

As such, we begin with the same man, the bassist on both those albums: Paul Chambers. He had taken up the bass a decade earlier in his adopted home of Detroit (where he was a student at the seminal Cass Technical High School ... more on that later). He arrived in New York in 1954 at 19. By the time of Kind of Blue and Giant Steps, he had been on over 100 sessions from dozens of leaders, with multiple dates under Davis (with whom he had started working in late 1955) and Coltrane (who had used him for several albums in 1957-58 as well as both fellow sideman for many others and Chambers also hiring Coltrane for his own sessions). In addition to the five albums he led, Chambers played on sessions for Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller, J.J. Johnson, Lee Morgan, Red Garland, Sonny Clark, and Sonny Rollins.

The collaboration between Davis and Chambers was remarkably fruitful before and after Kind of Blue and solidified a part of Davis' music that had previously seen widely differing players like Tommy Potter, Oscar Pettiford, Al McKibbon, and Percy Heath. The rest of 1959 saw multiple engagements around the country and closed with recordings that would be part of another monumental record, Sketches of Spain, that paired Davis' group with the Gil Evans Orchestra. 1960 continued that momentum with more Sketches of Spain recording and almost non-stop touring, including two stretches in Europe, from Spring onward. 1961 and 1962 had more of the same activity, the documents being Someday My Prince Will Come and Quiet Nights. Then, quite suddenly, Chambers left Davis' group in early February 1963.

It should be stated that Chambers did not restrict his activities solely to Davis, recording over four dozen albums during the period with, among many others, Jackie McLean, Wynton Kelly, Benny Golson, Hank Mobley, and Curtis Fuller. And after leaving Davis, he worked steadily with an array of leaders through the end of 1968, sadly passing away from tuberculosis caused and/or aggravated by drug abuse at only 33.

Stepping right into the Davis group was another Cass Technical High School alumnus: Ron Carter. Nearly 26, Carter was already prophesying his prolific career, participating in over three dozen albums since 1960, with the likes of Charli Persip, Yusef Lateef, Eric Dolphy, Don Ellis, Coleman Hawkins, Cecil Payne, Jaki Byard, Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Tadd Dameron, Dizzy Reece, Ken McIntyre, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson and others, plus waxing his leader debut, Where?, for Prestige subsidiary New Jazz in 1961.

It was Carter's arrival that heralded Davis' soon-to-be seminal band, though it took until Fall 1964 for its personnel to solidify. With Carter, Davis recorded Seven Steps To Heaven and played the Antibes festival in 1963. What is interesting though is while the "second great quintet" is thought of as a monolith, the bass chair had some upheaval/fluidity, depending on how you look at it. Gary Peacock - already a veteran and likely the only person to work for both Bud Shank and Albert Ayler - took the chair for nearly six weeks in the spring of 1964, Carter returning thereafter through the end of the year. 1965 began auspiciously with the January recording of E.S.P. but then things derailed with a convalescing Davis unable to play. And when he could, in November and December, Carter, a hot commodity, was absent, spelled by Peacock once more, then Reggie Workman, who had come up around the same time as Carter and had already come and gone in the groups of Coltrane. In 1966, Carter would return to the group but only partially, participating in East Coast performances, shows elsewhere having either Richard Davis, Carter's only real equal in terms of fecundity, or in the Peacock mold of eclecticism, Eddie Gomez, returning permanently in October, just before the album Miles Smiles. 1967 was similar: Carter was on board when not busy elsewhere, Gomez on call, then Albert Stinson for one show (a little over two years before his passing - see Bass Tragedies column in Issue 94) and then another veteran, Buster Williams, for a tour (and playing on one track of the 1981-released compilation album Directions). Carter would fill a fixed point for all of 1967, including the albums Sorcerer and Nefertiti and would continue with Davis through the middle of 1968.

Like Chambers or perhaps even more so, Carter was also on the greater jazz scene during his tenure with Davis. He recorded on sessions led by his fellow Davis bandmates but also by everyone from Bobby Timmons, Charles Lloyd, Donald Byrd and Bobby Hutcherson to Jimmy Smith, Shirley Scott, Eddie Harris, and Stanley Turrentine, to name only a handful. He has, of course, gone on to be likely the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

Paul Chambers' time under Coltrane was shorter and more intermittent. After Giant Steps he was part of, along with the rest of Davis' period band, November 1959 recordings that would partly comprise Coltrane Jazz and be brought back 18 months later as one of three individual bassists taking part in the Africa/Brass recordings (though his contribution was only heard on the 1995 complete sessions version).

Also in 1959 was a Birdland engagement for Coltrane where either Ahmed Abdul-Malik or George Tucker, both established and close in age to Coltrane, were on bass.

In 1960 Coltrane hired the slightly younger Steve Davis in what seems to be his first professional engagement. Davis stayed in the band through the end of the year for all its live dates and played on music recorded in October and released piecemeal on My Favorite Things, Coltrane Jazz, Coltrane Plays the Blues, and Coltrane's Sound. Though Davis lived until 1987, his credits after Coltrane were slight: the Mangione Brothers, Dave Burns, McCoy Tyner, Kenny Dorham, James Moody, Freddie McCoy, and Eddie Jefferson, all made in the '60s. One deviation in the year came via Coltrane's shared date with Don Cherry, The Avant-Garde, where bass was handled by either Charlie Haden or Percy Heath.

1961 was a year in flux, bassist-wise, for Coltrane. He introduced a concept to which he would return later in the decade by using two bassists for an engagement at Chicago's Sutherland Lounge in March: Raphael Don Garrett and Workman, the former, about six years younger, working with Roland Kirk, Paul Serrano, and Eddie Harris, the latter 11 years younger, sideman for Gigi Gryce, Donald Byrd, Duke Jordan, Richard Williams, and Dave Pike.

Workman would be part of the aforementioned Africa/Brass, as would, separately, another bassist, Art Davis, already with credits under Max Roach, Lee Morgan, Booker Little, Hal Mooney, Ernestine Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Leo Wright, Clifford Jordan/Sonny Red, Abbey Lincoln, and Booker Little. But in May they were together for Ole Coltrane and nearly a month at the Village Vanguard in August. Workman would become the fixed bassist for Coltrane through the end of the year for concerts, including a European tour, and a small portion of the Ballads album from the end of the year. An exception was Workman either alternating or alongside Jimmy Garrison for a November stint at the Village Vanguard.

If not for a family health crisis forcing Workman to leave the group at the end of 1961 and return to his native Philadelphia, he likely would have stayed with the band and jazz history been quite different. It should be said that Workman hardly is a footnote, becoming one of the most revered players of his generation. But it was Garrison who became the anchor. Born between Garrett and Workman, prior to joining Coltrane he had worked with Philly Joe Jones, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Dorham, Jackie McLean, JR Montrose, Walter Bishop, Jr., Ornette Coleman, Bill Barron, and Ted Curson.

Unlike Carter and Davis, once Garrison was on board, he stayed there. That was mostly to do with Coltrane's packed schedule of touring and albums and that, unlike Davis, he was healthy and non-combustible. From 1962-1964, Garrison was omnipresent, including the bulk of Ballads, Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (where he split duties with Ellington's period bassist Aaron Bell), 2018 discovery Both Directions At Once, John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman, Impressions, Crescent, another new millennium unearthed gem in Blue World, and closing out the year with Coltrane's magnum opus A Love Supreme (which added Art Davis for a second day of recording, released as a second disc to the album's deluxe edition in 2002).

In 1965 Garrison was still the main man but occasionally Davis would be alongside him: partially on The John Coltrane Quartet Plays in February and fully for June's Ascension. Otherwise, Garrison was the sole bassist for performances and most of the other albums: Transition, Sun Ship, and Meditations. The exceptions without Davis were overdubs of Haden for the posthumously released Infinity and Garrett returning to play both bass and clarinet for Live In Seattle (as well as the 2021 archival release A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle), Om, and part of Kulu Se Mama.

1966 was even more Garrison-centric, with the only documented work including a second bassist shows in November and December with Lionel "Sonny" Johnson, the brother of Dewey Johnson, who had played on Ascension. The last year of Coltrane's life, Garrison was there as well, with one notable absence: the Coltrane/Rashied Ali duet Interstellar Space.

Unlike Chambers or Carter, Garrison was kept so busy during his time with Coltrane that his outside discography at the time is meager, though it does include his sole leader date, Illumination! with the Elvin Jones/Jimmy Garrison Sextet. Otherwise it was sessions with Lorez Alexandria, Coltrane bandmate McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Bill Dixon, and Robert F. Pozar.

After Coltrane's death, Garrison kept working but his documentation slowed, his two Blue Note dates with the Jones trio rounded out by Joe Farrell being the most enduring. There were also dates with Rolf and Joachim Kuhn, Clifford Thornton and Nathan Davis, and regular work with Alice Coltrane and Archie Shepp. His final recording came in early 1975 with Beaver Harris and Dave Burrell's 360 Degree Music Experience. Garrison died of lung cancer in 1976 at 42.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Franck Carducci, playing music based on the progressive foundations of Pink Floyd and Genesis, moved to Amsterdam to play and survive. Theatrical prog rock, heavy rock reminiscent of Genesis and Led Zeppelin."Sheeple," with its bleating and swirling organ, evokes Pink Floyd and Deep Purple, forcing us to revisit the genre. "Self-Righteousness" boasts a raw, 70s sound, reminiscent of Whitesnake's old-school, fruity hard rock, with the dripping organ of this band playing good old-school, uncensored music. Barth unleashes a heavy, bulldozing solo. "Sweet Cassandra," the first of three tracks, features a narrative French-Anglican voice, while the harmonica, reminiscent of Supertramp, provides a soothing ballad. A nostalgic, sentimental tune that resonates. "The Betrayal of Blue," already heard on the 2023 live album. A Beatles-esque crescendo with an explosive verse, C�dric's oozing organ, Lea's furious pads, and Barth daring to play a solo reminiscent of bygone days?this young upstart is very good, navigating between two unique musical facets. The alternation of early heavy prog, with Mary's melting theremin break before the martial reprise, pads worthy of Genesis and Deep Purple. The exhilarating final crescendo flirts with the Wallian era, modern and old overlapping with the little dancer in her bottle?a touch of nostalgia. "Sweet Cassandra," a reprise with its Gabriel-esque flute, its marshmallow melody, a charismatic bucolic atmosphere."The Limits of Freedom," a chilling Genesis-like intro, a popular hard rock variation. A fresh, melodic interplay, a no-nonsense nod to a time before prog metal existed. Franck's other, more powerful rock side plays out its two distinct styles with his mischievous sidekick, featuring a frenetic guitar solo and a frenetic piano finale reminiscent of certain American bands. "Love or Survive" has a Supertramp-esque flavor, with its charming melody, piano, and subtly woven female backing vocals. It builds to a gradual crescendo, culminating in a seemingly endless bluesy guitar solo that evokes the emotion of yesteryear. The basic break, with its raw vocals and piano, transforms into an old-fashioned melody. The thunderous organ kicks in, providing a Beatles-esque chorus to conclude this crescendo, a musical comedy of guitar and organ intertwined. "Sweet Cassandra" returns to the bar scene named after Cassandra, ending with a syrupy vocal, creating suspense before launching into "Do What You're Told," bringing the band back to its acoustic melody worthy of Oldfield. Franck is hardly inventing anything new in revisiting our classics. A prominent bass, a southern feel, piano bar rock to free us from societal constraints and finally do what we want before the end of time.

items.body: In giving this album a listen, it is difficult not to jump between the original recordings of the great Blossom Dearie, and those newly recorded by modern-day pianist/vocalist Dawn Clement. After all, those who have followed Clement's career have heard the comparisons between the two, particularly the vocal style that those critiquing Dearie referred to as "distinctive," "light," and "girlish." The separator here is that Dearie, while lauded for her original piano style, is more renowned for her colorful, poetic vocals. Clement has thrived in both ways, but is perhaps better known for her powerful, rhythmic and harmonically brilliant original work on piano. The vocal side of her artistry features a wide-ranging, pitch- perfect instrument that has put the finishing touches on the "unique" part of her musical profile. All of this being said, it would seem likely then that Dear Ms. Dearie (Origin, 2026) would be a satisfying listen, and indeed, it is. There is no dressing things up here, as Clement works her way through fifteen tunes favored by Dearie, with an all-star presence in the studio to assist. Bassist John Clayton and drummer Jeff Hamilton are the perfect complement to this project, able to keep the session swinging at any tempo and in any time signature. Clement's Colorado mate Steve Kovalcheck jumps in on guitar to complete a live-in-the-studio sound that pulls you in for a more intimate listen. "The Gentleman is a Dope" leads things off, with Clement taking the tune in on piano, establishing the easy swing of her bandmates. Clement does not skip a beat, entering the fray singing the first verse. She gathers things together following Kovalcheck's breakneck solo, before releasing the flow of the melody to the end of the tune. If there is a parallel for starters between the artist and subject here, it is the feeling that the piano and the voice are one thing, of one mind. There is a clear advantage of a singer accompanying themselves, knowing best how to complement the vocal component of their artistry. There is no overplaying or other missteps to be concerned with. Clement's voice darts between notes of the melody in the same bop cadence of her melodic playing on piano. The lead tune reveals the sincerity that takes a perfectly solid performance and makes it exceptional. "Figure 8" is a tune familiar to those who grew up in the early 1970s watching Saturday morning cartoons. As the theme song for the educational "Schoolhouse Rock" series, youngsters were exposed to Dearie singing Bob McDonough's wispy math- inspired lyrics. Accompanied by the full chords of Kovalcheck and bassist Clayton's elegant bow work, Clement lightly escorts the tune to a higher tempo, adding scant comping while Kovalcheck carries the harmonic load. "Once Upon a Summertime" is the title tune from Dearie's 1959 Verve Records classic. It is here that Clement's work is illuminated visually, the nostalgic lyrics brightly revealed like landscapes captured by an artist on a bright sunny day. Clement works in tandem with Clayton, offering a stunning solo that flows out of her dynamic sense of emotion within harmony. The ballad may just be the high point of the session, although it is presented as the twelfth track of the fifteen. No tip of the cap to Dearie would be complete without a version of the David Frishberg penned "I'm Hip," again with lyrics from McDonough. Clayton's walking bass line and Hamilton's sublime brushwork lay down the foundation for Clement's swinging, fleeting treatment of every syllable. Kovalcheck's work throughout the session is perfectly complementary to the other chordal instrument, allowing both he and Clement to play unforced, with an emphasis on beauty and intimacy. On all fifteen tunes, Clement does not have to force a darn thing, her natural musical self fits so perfectly into the spirit of Dearie's work and legacy. While adhering to the simple, straight-ahead setting present on the original classic recordings, Clement makes the music quite naturally hers, perhaps finally eschewing the label of being a pianist who also sings. Those in the know are aware that this has never been the case. Dearie once stated that she did not like singing or playing piano separately. It feels that way throughout the playlist that Clement offers here. Dear Ms. Dearie may not be Clement's best album to date in terms of her career as a highly original jazz pianist. It is indeed a departure from her preceding trio effort, Delight (Origin, 2025), with Buster Williams and Matt Wilson—but it may be the best manifestation of her complete musical presence revealed.

items.body:
Wiki returns with 'Right Away', a cloud rap/drill hybrid that's backed with the beatless slow-burner 'Park'.

It's hard to believe that it's been three years since we last heard from Wiki. He dropped '14K Figaro', going head-to-head with MIKE-collaborator Tony Seltzer and then went dark. Sure, he might have been spotted in 'Marty Supreme', but that hardly counts, does it? Well, 'Right Away' was worth the wait; production-wise it's a curiosity, rhythmically indebted to drill but lightened by Silky Johnson-style smeared samples. And Wiki's in his zone, twisting his tongue around the snaps like he's got a foot between Kodak Black and A$AP Rocky.
items._cn_summary: Wiki 回归新作《Right Away》是一张云说唱与drill风格融合的嘻哈作品，节奏框架承袭drill传统，但以Silky Johnson式的涂抹化采样加以柔化处理。另一首收录曲《Park》则是一首去节拍化的慢燃型曲目。Wiki的说唱风格被描述为在Kodak Black与A$AP Rocky之间找到了自己的位置，以灵活的口语节奏驾驭密集的鼓点编排。整体而言，这是一张植根于纽约地下嘻哈场景的作品，与实验音乐、前卫爵士、电子声响等领域的关联极为有限，对于关注实验与跨界融合的听众来说缺乏足够的吸引力。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Unlike many Basque bands from northern Spain that seek artistic autonomy in every possible way, THESOULBREAKER COMPANY from Vitoria-Gasteiz has strived to cut off all its traditional ties and viedfor the prize to emerge as the most American sounding band in the entire nation. This band got itsstart in 2003 as a six piece that has emerged over the ensuing decades as one of the nation's mostdiverse jazzy / heavy / psychedelic progressive bands but in the beginning was more focused onsounding like a modern rendition of a 70s heavy blues rock band mixed with the stoner rock andgrunge sensibilities of the 1990s USA. Debuting in 2005, the band released its first album HOT SMOKE& HEAVY BLUES which by the title alone will pretty much tell you what you're in store for with thisone. Album #1 is a collection of eleven tracks that extend to a more modern playing time of 55 minuteshowever unlike some of its influences that include a wide swath of older bands such as Led Zeppelin,Captain Beyond, and Grand Funk Railroad from the 70s and Queens of the Stone Age, Monster Magnet,the Black Crowes and even Soundgarden from the 90s, THE SOULBREAKER COMPANY featured a much largerlineup which has remained mostly stable over two decades time. This album features lead vocalist /acoustic guitarist Jony Moreno, the two guitarists Daniel Tri�anes and Asier Fern�ndez, bassist J.J.Manzanedo, keyboardist Oscar Gil (Txiki Lazyhand) and drummer / percussionist Andoni Ortiz(Domingo). While the band would develop its psychedelic and progressive attributes throughout itscareer, on this debut the musical style is pretty much limited to short heavy bluesy rock trackssounding like a tribute to the aforementioned acts in full street savvy bravado.With all lyrics delivered in English with an eye for the international market, THE SOULBREAKERCOMPANY sounds like a throwback to a time long past with its heavy guitar-driven rock boogieshuffling along with vintage psychedelic influences finding their way into organ swells. While theband's overall sound evokes the classic 70s rock scene, the tones and production are morereminiscent of the 90s Palm Desert stoner rock scene with bands like Kyuss and Queens of The StoneAge providing the primary influences. While the band is lacking any clear original stamp at thispoint, these guys honed their chops well and sound like they really could've emerged from the PalmSprings area of California circa 1992 with a bar fight ready soundtrack for a bunch of good ole boyshaving a few too many at the local pub. It's honestly about as retro as it gets. Despite all theother influences i hear a distinct Black Crowes lilt in the vocalist's style however the ChisCornell / Soundgarden worship is in the forefront.While the logical point of entry to explore the band's discography, for anyone seeking the moreprogressive and psychedelic space rock styles of the band, this is clearly not the place for you asthis album basically establishes the band as a heavy hitting blues rock band looking to the past forits wellspring of inspiration. The psychedelic attributes would ramp up on the band's second album"The Pink Alchemist" while the progressive touches would bloom on the third "�taca." Overall there'snothing new under the sun here and if you're seeking some well performed retro blues rock on theheavier side of the spectrum then HOT SMOKE & HEAVY BLUES may suit you well but honestly this stylewas played out by the mid-90s and while i do not dislike a more basic heavy blues rock, i'd muchprefer experiencing the original acts that developed these sounds in the first place. All in allit's a decent debut but at this stage the band was basically a mimicry and not ready for itscreative primetime.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自西班牙巴斯克地区Vitoria-Gasteiz的六人乐队The Soulbreaker Company的2005年首张专辑，以复古的硬蓝调摇滚为基调，融合了70年代齐柏林飞艇式重摇滚、90年代棕榈沙漠stoner rock和垃圾摇滚的影响。整体呈现为吉他驱动的摇滚boogie，辅以风琴铺底的迷幻点缀，乐手技术扎实但评论明确指出乐队在此阶段缺乏原创性印记，听感类似加州酒吧打架前的背景配乐。巴斯克地区出身为其增添了一层非主流地域色彩，但乐队刻意割裂传统音乐联系、刻意追求美式声音取向，使得专辑缺少独特的文化视角。与实验前卫、自由爵士、电子、暗潮等用户偏好领域几乎无交集。

items.body: At a time when economics often dictates the size and scope of a jazz group, adding a guitarist to a typical piano-bass-drums trio makes a world of difference. And when said guitarist is Peter Bernstein, the difference is even more pronounced. That gives bassist Harvie S a clear headstart on Bright Dawn, a modest studio date with Bernstein broadening the usual trio setting on the bassist's 21st recording as leader of his own ensemble—the first, however, following a 15-year hiatus. The other members of Harvie's group, each of whom plays a pivotal role, are pianist Miki Hayama (Fender Rhodes on "Ghosts of Havana" and "Voice in the Sky") and drummer Matt Wilson who introduces and sparks the perky "I've Got Rhythm and Blues." That is one of Harvie's eight compositions, escorting Bob Dorough's playful "Devil May Care" and Chick Corea's sunny "Humpty Dumpty." And therein lies the session's most problematic aspect. Even though decent and well-intentioned, Harvie's compositions are, to be frank, several lengthy strides away from memorable. While that may be traced in part to the group's makeup and Harvie S's resolve to lead the way, the fact remains that the success of any collective enterprise, regardless of size or shape, rests in large measure on its choice of material, and most of the songs on Bright Dawn simply don't measure up, even with Bernstein on board to help enliven them. Harvie must be given props for naming one of his themes "Navalny" (and enhancing it with arco and string bass) but even that melody seems tame when compared to what comes next, the spunky "Rhythm and Blues," one of the session's few high spots. Hayama is an impressive soloist, as is Bernstein, and their expertise must be noted. That is not, however, nearly enough to raise Bright Dawn above the norm.
